🩸 The 'Petach' of an Uncertain Woman — between seven and seventeen clean days to resolve her status
❓ Purity for Her Husband vs. Resolving Her Category — why seven days alone isn't enough
🏠 Quarantine for Leprous Marks — one week for a person, up to three weeks for a house
📅 A Closing List of Minimums and Maximums — intercalated months, the two loaves, showbread, and brit mila

overview.title: 📖 Overview: A Chapter of Minimums and Maximums
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 8a–8b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין פֶּתַח בְּטוֹעָה פָּחוֹת מִשִּׁבְעָה, וְלֹא יָתֵר עַל שִׁבְעָה עָשָׂר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes the discussion of a poor man's two valuation vows made in one breath, left unresolved as teiku, and then turns to a run of mishnayot each structured just like the arakhin mishna: 'no less than X, no more than Y.' A woman uncertain whether her bleeding fell in her days of menstruation or the eleven days of ziva needs between seven and seventeen clean days to resolve her status, depending on how many days she bled; the Gemara clarifies this range is not about her permission to her husband, which is always resolved within seven days, but about pinning down her halakhic category. Marks of leprosy require a minimum one-week quarantine for a person and can take up to three weeks for a house, prompting Rav Pappa's homiletic reading of a psalm. The daf closes with a fresh mishna listing several more such ranges: the number of thirty-day months added to a year, the days within which the two loaves and the showbread must be eaten, and the earliest and latest day for a circumcision.

slides.title: 🪙 Two Simultaneous Valuation Vows — Splitting the Five Sela
slides.subtitle: Continuing yesterday's case of a poor man with only five sela

steps.content: 1️⃣ Recap: paying the SECOND vow first (4 of 5 sela), then the FIRST vow (the last 1) fulfills both — 'a later creditor who collects first keeps what he collected'
2️⃣ But paying the FIRST vow with 4 sela and the SECOND with the last 1: the second is fulfilled, but the first is NOT — all 5 were available when it alone was due

3️⃣ New dilemma (Rav Adda bar Ahava): if he vows BOTH valuations in one breath, so they take effect simultaneously, do the 5 sela split evenly — 2½ toward each — or does each vow independently claim all 5?
4️⃣ The Gemara leaves this open: תֵּיקוּ — unresolved

slides.title: 🩸 The 'Petach' of an Uncertain Woman — How Many Clean Days?
slides.subtitle: A woman unsure whether her bleeding fell in her days of niddah or her days of ziva
rows: Worst case: that single day could be the very start of a new cycle
Could span the end of her ziva days into the start of niddah
A longer bleed shortens the maximum possible remaining uncertainty
The longest bleed needs the fewest additional clean days to resolve

callout.label: The mishna's headline:
callout.text: Whatever the count of days she bled, resolving her status never takes fewer than seven clean days, and never more than seventeen.

slides.title: ❓ Why Not Just Always Count Seven?
slides.subtitle: Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges the whole elaborate system

lines.speaker: R' Adda
lines.text: Why all this counting? Let her simply count seven clean days and be permitted to her husband, as any woman may!

lines.speaker: Rabba
lines.text: We are not asking about her permission to her husband — that IS always resolved within seven days. We are asking a separate question: is she a niddah or a zava?

lines.speaker: R' Adda presses
lines.text: What difference does the label make, if she's permitted either way after seven?

lines.speaker: Rabba explains
lines.text: A great difference: if she is a niddah, she is pure after seven days regardless of how many are clean. If her bleeding fell during the days of ziva for one or two days, she is pure after just ONE clean day; for three or more, she needs seven — as a full zava.

callout.label: The real question:
callout.text: 'Petach' is not about marital purity — it is about pinning down which category she was ever in, a determination that can take up to seventeen days.

slides.title: 🏠 Quarantine for Leprous Marks — Person vs. House
slides.subtitle: The mishna's next 'no less, no more' pair

boxes.title: נִגְעֵי אָדָם (Marks on a Person)
items: A priest issues a definitive ruling after seven days

boxes.title: נִגְעֵי בָתִּים (Marks on a House)
items: Some house-mark cases require the full three weeks to resolve

callout.label: Rav Pappa's homiletic reading of Psalms 36:7:
callout.text: 'Your righteousness is like the mighty mountains' — the quick, one-week resolution for a person; 'Your judgments are like the great deep' — the extended, three-week uncertainty of a house. The Gemara ties this to a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina over how God weighs merit against sin.

slides.title: 📅 A Closing List of Minimums and Maximums
slides.subtitle: The new mishna extends the 'no less, no more' pattern across several unrelated halakhot
rows: Thirty-day months added to a year

summary.principle: Just as a valuation vow is bounded between one sela and fifty, the mishna shows that Jewish law repeatedly frames uncertainty and timing within a fixed floor and ceiling — a woman's clean days, a leprous mark's quarantine, a calendar's intercalated months, and the eating window for the Temple's breads and the timing of a brit mila.

flowSteps.content: 🪙 A poor man's two simultaneous valuation vows: how to split five sela between them — left as teiku
🩸 An uncertain woman's clean-day count runs from seven to seventeen, resolving her CATEGORY, not merely her permission to her husband

columns.content: 🏠 Nega'im: one week minimum for a person, up to three weeks for a house
📅 New mishna: intercalated months, the two loaves, showbread, and brit mila each get their own floor and ceiling

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: halakha frequently bounds uncertainty between a fixed minimum and maximum rather than leaving it open-ended

quiz.q: In Rav Adda bar Ahava's unresolved dilemma, what are the two possibilities if a poor man with five sela vows two valuations simultaneously?
o: He pays two and a half sela toward each vow, OR all five sela are considered fully available to each vow (so he owes five for each)
He is entirely exempt from both vows
He must pay ten sela total regardless
Only the first vow is valid; the second is meaningless
quiz.e: The Gemara raises exactly this dilemma — since the vows took effect together, does the sum split evenly, or does each vow independently claim the whole amount? — and leaves it as teiku.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what is the minimum and maximum number of clean days needed to resolve a woman's uncertain status between the days of niddah and ziva?
o: A minimum of one day, no maximum
A minimum of seven clean days, a maximum of seventeen
Always exactly seven days, no variation
A minimum of eleven days, a maximum of thirty
quiz.e: The mishna states plainly: 'there is no petach for an uncertain woman of fewer than seven, and not more than seventeen.'

quiz.q: According to Rabba's answer to Rav Adda bar Ahava, why isn't it enough for the uncertain woman to simply count seven clean days?
o: Because seven days is never sufficient for any purpose in this case
Because permission to her husband is always resolved within seven days, but the extended count is needed to determine which category — niddah or zava — she actually falls into
Because the Torah requires exactly seventeen days for every menstruating woman
Because Rabba disagreed with the entire premise of the mishna
quiz.e: Rabba clarifies that the mishna's extended range addresses resolving her halakhic status (niddah vs. zava), a separate question from her permission to her husband, which is always settled within seven days.

quiz.q: What is the difference in quarantine length between leprous marks on a person and leprous marks on a house?
o: A person's marks require a minimum of one week; a house's marks can require up to three weeks
Both require exactly the same three-week quarantine
A house requires only one day; a person requires three weeks
Neither has any fixed quarantine period
quiz.e: The Gemara explains the mishna's 'no less than one week' refers to marks on a person, and 'no more than three weeks' refers to marks on a house.

quiz.q: According to the mishna at the end of the daf, within what range of days must the showbread (lechem hapanim) be eaten from when it was baked?
o: Between two and three days
Between nine and eleven days
Between four and eight days
Between eight and twelve days
quiz.e: The mishna states the showbread is eaten no earlier than the ninth day from baking and no later than the eleventh day, depending on how the Festival calendar falls that week.
